subject: psychology
title: Memory: Types of LTM & Forgetting
welcome_lead: Tulving says memory has flavours — and forgetting comes in two main kinds.
meta_desc: A-Level Psychology LTM types Tulving 1985, interference and retrieval failure forgetting.
final_note: Forgetting is a clue to how memory is organised, not just a failure.

concepts.def: Time-stamped autobiographical events with context and emotion.
General knowledge of facts, meanings and concepts.
Memory for motor skills — implicit and hard to verbalise.
Forgetting where similar memories disrupt each other.
Cue-dependent forgetting when cues at encoding are absent at recall.
Tulving 1983 — recall is best when cues match encoding context.

walkthroughs.body_html: Tulving (1985) argued LTM is not unitary: episodic (your first day at school), semantic (Paris is France's capital) and procedural (riding a bike). Brain scans show episodic uses the hippocampus, semantic the temporal lobe, procedural the cerebellum.

Proactive interference — old learning disrupts new. Retroactive interference — new learning disrupts old. McGeoch & McDonald (1931) showed similar word lists caused most interference; Baddeley & Hitch (1977) found rugby players forgot more games when they had played more, not when more time had passed.

Tulving's encoding specificity principle: cues at encoding aid recall. Godden & Baddeley (1975) divers recalled 40% more when recall context matched learning (land/water). State-dependent forgetting works the same way for mood or drug state.
